questiontext.text:
The Aphel Stem: Divine Action & Causative Verbs

ܐܦܥܠ ʾaphel

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 1: Review of Lessons 1–4

questiontext.text:
Section 1: Review of Lessons 1–4

Quick Summary

Before diving into the Aphel stem, let’s review the foundational material from the first four lessons:

  • Lesson 0: The Estrangela alphabet, letter order, and the non-joining letters.

  • Lesson 1: The noun system (gender, number, and the absolute, construct, and emphatic states), independent pronouns, verbless clauses, and the particles d- (relative/possessive) and l- (to/for, direct object).

  • Lesson 2: The Peal stem and its active participle. With enclitic pronouns, the participle forms the narrative present (kāteb-nā, “I am writing”).

  • Lesson 3: The Peal perfect (suffix conjugation) of ܟܬܒ (k-t-b, ‘write’), V-S-O narrative word order, and the conjunction w-.

  • Lesson 4: Pronominal suffixes on nouns and prepositions, and the idiom ʾit l- for “to have”.

5-Question Warm-Up Drill

Answer these questions using what you’ve learned. Answers are in Section 9.

  1. ܟܬܒ — Give the 3rd m.sg. Peal perfect and its meaning.

  2. What are the three states of the Syriac noun? Give an example of each.

  3. Translate: ܗܘ ܪܒܐ ܗܘ (hū rabbā hū)

  4. What does the Peal active participle of ܐܙܠ (ʾ-z-l, ‘go’) look like, m.sg.?

  5. Identify the root and stem of the form ܟܬܒܬ (ketbat)
Warm-up 1. What is the 3rd m.sg. Peal perfect of ܟܬܒ, and what does it mean?

feedback.text: Correct: the bare root with the a-a pattern.
That is 3 f.sg.; the 3 m.sg. has no suffix.
That is the participle, not the perfect.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 2. Which list gives the three states of the Syriac noun?

feedback.text: Syriac nouns have no case endings; states do that work.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 3. Translate: ܗܘ ܪܒܐ ܗܘ (hū rabbā hū)

feedback.text: Correct: a verbless clause, the second hū acting as copula.
The second hū is the copula, not a relative clause.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 4. What is the Peal active participle m.sg. of ܐܙܠ (ʾ-z-l, 'go')?

feedback.text: The m- prefix belongs to derived-stem participles, not the Peal.
The -ā ending marks the f.sg. participle.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 5. Identify the form ܟܬܒܬ (ketbat).

answer.text: Root k-t-b, Peal perfect, 3 f.sg., 'she wrote'

feedback.text: Correct: -at is the 3 f.sg. ending. (Unvocalized, ܟܬܒܬ can also be 2 m.sg. or 1 c.sg.; the vowels ketbat settle it.)
The Aphel would add the ʾa- prefix.
The final ܬ is a suffix, not a root letter.

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 2: The Derived Stems — Overview

questiontext.text:
Section 2: The Derived Stems — Overview

One of the most powerful features of Semitic languages — shared by Syriac, Hebrew, and Arabic — is the system of derived verbal stems. A single three-consonant root can generate multiple verbs with systematically related meanings, simply by modifying the vowel pattern and/or adding prefixes or affixes.

This is very different from Greek or Latin, where related meanings usually require entirely different words. In Syriac, once you know a root, you already know the building blocks of an entire semantic family.

The Three Major Active Stems

Stem Name Formation Pattern Basic Meaning Shift Example
Peal Basic vowel pattern Basic action / state ܟܬܒ — katab, ‘he wrote’
Paael Middle root letter doubled Intensive / Factitive ܩܕܫ — qaddaš, ‘he sanctified’
Aphel ʾa- prefix added Causative ܐܚܝܝ — ʾaḥyī, ‘he caused to live’

Cross-Linguistic Comparison

For those coming from Hebrew or Arabic, these correspondences will look familiar:

Syriac Peal Paael Aphel
Hebrew Qal Piel Hiphil
Arabic Form I Form II Form IV
Function Basic Intensive/Factitive Causative

For learners with a Greek background: Greek uses voice (active, middle, passive) and aspect to express some of these distinctions, but there is no exact parallel to the Semitic derived stem system. The Greek causative construction (e.g., ποιεῖν + infinitive) expresses what the Aphel does morphologically. Latin similarly uses circumlocutions (facere + infinitive) or prefix verbs for some causative senses.

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 3: The Aphel Stem

questiontext.text:
Section 3: The Aphel Stem

Core Meaning: Causative

The Aphel stem expresses causative action — ‘to cause X to happen’ or ‘to make X do Y.’ In theological language, this is the stem of divine action: God ʾaḥyī (gave life), God ʾaglī (revealed), God ʾaqreb (brought near).

Formation

  • Perfect: ʾa- prefix + CeCC pattern (same person suffixes as Peal perfect)

  • Participle: m- prefix + CaCC-eC pattern (cf. Peal participle)

Comparison with Other Languages

  • Hebrew Hiphil: prefix הִ/הֶ (hi-/he-) added to the root. E.g., ḥāyāh (live) → heḥĕyāh (give life); qārab (draw near) → hiqrīb (bring near/offer). The structural parallel to Syriac Aphel is very close.

  • Arabic Form IV: ʾa- prefix + CaCaCa → ʾaCCaCa. E.g., ḫaraja (go out) → ʾaḫraja (bring out); qāraba (approach) → ʾaqraba (bring near). The Syriac Aphel prefix ʾa- is cognate with Arabic Form IV.

  • Greek/Latin: No direct morphological equivalent. Greek uses prefix verbs (e.g., ζωοποιεῖν, ‘to give life’) or constructions with ποιεῖν + inf. Latin uses facere + infinitive or prefix verbs.

Aphel Examples: Peal → Aphel

Peal (Syr) Root Peal Meaning Aphel (Syr) Aphel Translit Aphel Meaning
ܚܝܝ ḥ-y-y ’t o live’ ܐܚ ܝܝ *ʾaḥyī (Peal) * ’to give lif e, save’
ܩܪܒ q-r-b ’ to draw ܐ ܩܪܒ *ʾaqr near’ (Peal) eb* ’to bring ne ar, offer’
ܦܩ n-p-q ’to go ܐܦܩ *ʾa out’ (Peal) ppeq* ’to bring out, produce’
ܢܦܠ n-p-l ’t o fall’ ܐܦ ܠ *ʾappe (Peal) l* ’to cause to f all, throw down’

The ʾAlap-Lamed-Peh Root (ʾ-l-p) in the Aphel

The root ܐܠܦ (ʾ-l-p) means ‘learn’ in the Peal stem. In the Aphel, it means ‘to teach’ — that is, ‘to cause someone to learn.’ This root will be used for all paradigm tables in Sections 4–5.
What basic meaning does the Aphel stem add to a root?
Which stem in Hebrew and Arabic corresponds to the Syriac Aphel?

answer.text: Hebrew Hiphil and Arabic Form IV

feedback.text: Correct: all three are causative, and the Arabic ʾa- prefix is cognate.

answer.text: Hebrew Piel and Arabic Form II
Hebrew Qal and Arabic Form I
Hebrew Niphal and Arabic Form VII

questiontext.text: The root ܐܠܦ means 'learn' in the Peal. What does it mean in the Aphel?

feedback.text: That would be an intensive sense, not causative.

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 4: Aphel Perfect Paradigm

questiontext.text:
Section 4: Aphel Perfect Paradigm

Root: ʾ-l-p | Stem: Aphel | Meaning: ‘to teach’

ܐܦܥܠ Perfect — Full Conjugation

Person Estrangela Transliteration Translation
3 m.sg. ܐܠܦ ʾalep he ta ught
3 f.sg. ܐܠܦܬ *ʾallpa t* she taught
2 m.sg. ܐܠܦܬ *ʾalept * you (m.sg .) taught
2 f.sg. ܐܠܦܬܝ *ʾalepti * you (f.sg .) taught
1 c.sg. ܐܠܦܬ *ʾallpe t* I t aught
3 m.pl. ܐܠܦܘ *ʾallpū * they (m .) taught
3 f.pl. ܐܠܦܝ *ʾallpī * they (f .) taught
2 m.pl. ܐܠܦܬܘܢ *ʾaleptū n* you (m.pl .) taught
2 f.pl. ܐܠܦܬܝܢ *ʾalepti n* you (f.pl .) taught
1 c.pl. ܐܠܦܢ *ʾallpe n* we t aught

Formation Notes:

  • Prefix: ʾa- added before the root (3 m.sg.: ʾalep)

  • Root-internal vowel: e vowel between R2 and R3 in 3 m.sg.

  • Suffixes: Identical to Peal perfect suffixes (-at, -t, -ti, -et, -ū, -ī, -tūn, -tin, -n)

  • Note on gutturals: When R1 is Alaph (ʾ), assimilation or lengthening may occur in some forms

Comparison: Hebrew Hiphil Perfect

The Hebrew Hiphil perfect is structurally parallel to the Syriac Aphel perfect, with a causative prefix (הִ- hi-/הֶ- he-) and essentially the same suffix set:

Person Hebrew (Hiphil) Transliteration Translation
3 m.sg. הֶֽאֱמִין heʾĕmīn he believed (H. Hiphil of ʾ-m-n)
3 f.sg. הֶֽאֱמִינָה heʾĕmīnāh she believed
1 c.sg. הֶֽאֱמַנְתִּי heʾĕmantī I believed
3 m.pl. הֶֽאֱמִינוּ heʾĕmīnū they believed

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 4: Aphel Perfect Paradigm (continued)

questiontext.text:
Section 4: Aphel Perfect Paradigm (continued)

Comparison: Arabic Form IV Perfect

Arabic Form IV (ʾaCCaCa) is cognate with the Syriac Aphel. The prefix ʾa- and the causative meaning are identical; only the internal vowel pattern differs:

Person Arabic (Form IV) Transliteration Translation
3 m.sg. أَرْسَلَ ʾarsala he sent (Form IV of r-s-l)
3 f.sg. أَرْسَلَتْ ʾarsalat she sent
1 c.sg. أَرْسَلْتُ ʾarsaltu I sent
3 m.pl. أَرْسَلُوا ʾarsalū they sent

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 5: Aphel Participle Paradigm

questiontext.text:
Section 5: Aphel Participle Paradigm

Root: ʾ-l-p | Stem: Aphel | Meaning: ‘causing to learn / teaching’

The Aphel active participle expresses ongoing or habitual causative action. It also frequently serves as an adjective. The participle prefix is m- (as in all derived stems).

Form Estrangela Transliteration Translation
m.sg. (active) ܡܐܠܦ maʾlep teaching (m.sg.)
f.sg. (active) ܡܐܠܦܐ maʾlpā teaching (f.sg.)
m.pl. (active) ܡܐܠܦܝܢ maʾlpī n teaching (m.pl.)
f.pl. (active) ܡܐܠܦܢ maʾlpā n teaching (f.pl.)

Formation Notes

  • Prefix: m- added before the root (same prefix as Paael and other derived-stem participles)

  • Vowel pattern: maʾ- + R2 + vowel + R3 (cf. Peal participle kāteb → Aphel maʾlep)

  • Gender/number suffixes: Same as all Syriac participles: m.sg. (unmarked), f.sg. (-ā), m.pl. (-īn), f.pl. (-ān)

Comparison with Hebrew and Arabic

Hebrew Hiphil participle: prefix מַ/מֵ (ma-/me-). E.g., maʾămīn (believing/trusting — from ʾ-m-n Hiphil). The m- participle prefix is pan-Semitic.

Arabic Form IV active participle: pattern muCCiC. E.g., mursil (sending/sender — from ʾarsala). Note the Arabic Form IV participle has the vowel shift u-i, while Syriac uses a-e.

KEY PATTERN: In all Syriac derived stems, the participle prefix is m-. This is one of the most consistent features of Syriac verbal morphology. If you see a verb beginning with m- that is not a Peal form, suspect a derived-stem participle.
What prefix marks the participle in all the Syriac derived stems?

feedback.text: Correct: maʾlep 'teaching'. A non-Peal verb starting with m- is probably a participle.
n- is an imperfect prefix (1 c.pl.).

questiontext.text: Give the meaning of ܡܐܠܦܝܢ (maʾlpīn).

feedback.text: Correct: Aphel participle with the m.pl. ending -īn.
The emphatic m.pl. would end in -ē.

questiontext.text:
Section 6: Theological Vocabulary

Abstract Nouns and Key Theological Terms

The following twenty terms form the core theological vocabulary of early Syriac Christianity. Many are abstract nouns derived from the same roots as the verbs you are learning.

Estrangela Transliteration Meaning Notes
ܚܝܐ / ܦܘܪܩܢܐ ḥayye / purqānā s alvation / life (life/li Two overlapping terms; ḥayye ves, pl.) often = ‘eternal life’; purqānā = ‘redemption’
ܓܠܝܐ glāyā revelation, From Aphe disclosure l ʾaglī; cf. Gk apokalypsis, Lat revelatio
ܫܕܪܐ šedārā sending, miss ion From šadar ; cf. Heb šāliaḥ (envoy), Gk apostolos
ܒܪܝܬܐ brīttā creation From Peal brā ; cf. Heb bārāʾ, Gen 1:1
ܪܚܡܐ raḥmē mercy, Pl. of raḥmā compassion ; cognate with Heb raḥămīm, Arabic raḥma
ܕܝܢܐ dīnā judgment Cf. Heb dīn (legal judgment), Arabic dīn (religion/judgment)
ܫܘܒܚܐ šūbḥā glory, prais e Cf. Heb kābōd ; used in doxologies
ܛܝܒܘܬܐ ṭaybūtt ā grace, goodne ss Abstract nou n from ṭāb (good); cf. Gk charis, Latin gratia
ܗܝܡܢܘܬܐ haymānūt tā faith, trus t Abstract nou n from hayman; cf. Heb ʾĕmūnāh
ܟܐܢܘܬܐ kēnūtt ā righteousnes s, Cf. Gk dikai justice osynē, Heb ṣĕdāqāh
ܚܛܝܬܐ ḥṭīttā sin, Cf. Gk ha transgression martia, Heb ḥēṭ
ܡܥܡܘܕܝܬܐ maʿmūdīt tā baptism Lit. ’immers ion’; from ʿ-m-d; cf. Gk baptisma
ܨܠܘܬܐ ṣlūttā prayer From ṣ-l-y; cf. Heb tefillah
ܐܘܠܦܢܐ ʾūlpān ā teaching, Abstract nou instruction n from Aphel ʾalep
ܢܒܘܬܐ nebūtt ā prophecy From n-b-y; cf. Heb nĕbūʾāh, Gk prophēteia
ܩܝܡܐ qyāmā covenant, Double meanin resurrection g: covenant (cf. Heb bĕrīt) and resurrection
ܟܬܒܐ ktābā scripture, From k-t-b; writing cf. Arabic kitāb, Hebrew kĕtābīm
ܒܘܪܟܬܐ būrktā blessing From b-r-k; cf. Heb bĕrākāh, Arabic baraka
ܪܘܚܐ rūḥā spirit, wind , f. noun; cf breath . Heb rūaḥ, Arabic rūḥ, Gk pneuma
ܫܪܪܐ šrārā truth, reali ty Cf. Heb ʾĕmet , Gk alētheia; šrār = ‘to be firm/true’

Section 6: Theological Vocabulary (continued)

Key Aphel Verbs in Theological Context

Estrangela Translit Stem Meaning Usage Note
ܐܚܝܝ ʾaḥyī Aphel to save, give Causative of life ḥ-y-y (live); divine act par excellence
ܐܓܠܝ ʾaglī Aphel to reveal, Causative o uncover f g-l-y (be revealed); cf. Heb gillāh
ܫܕܪ šadar Peal/Aphel to send Common verb; šadar/ʾešdar; cf. Heb šālaḥ
ܒܪܐ brā Peal to create Note: in Sy riac this is Peal (not Aphel); cf. Heb bārāʾ
ܐܟܪܙ ʾkraz Aphel to proclaim, From k-r-z; preach kerygmatic vocabulary
ܐܪܝܡ ʾrīm Aphel to exalt, Causative of lift up r-m (be high); cf. Heb hērīm
ܐܫܦܠ ʾšpel Aphel to humble, Causative o lower f š-p-l (be low); antonym of ʾrīm
ܐܦܪܩ ʾpraq Aphel to redeem, Causative o deliver f p-r-q (be freed); cf. purqānā above
ܩܕܫ qaddaš Paael to sanctify, Preview of make holy Paael; from q-d-š (be holy); cf. Heb qiddēš
ܐܩܪܒ ʾaqreb Aphel to bring Causative of near, offer q-r-b (draw near); cf. Arabic qurraba
Which word means 'faith'?
ܩܝܡܐ (qyāmā) carries a double meaning. What are the two?

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 5 · Section 7: The Story — Part 5

questiontext.text:
Section 7: The Story — Part 5

Yukhannan Preaches to the Crowds

Narrative note: This passage features heavy use of the Aphel stem to describe God’s causative actions in history. Notice the verbless clauses used for theological assertions (sentences 6 and 9). Aphel forms are highlighted in the transliteration.

Key Aphel forms in this passage: ʾkraz (proclaimed), ʾalep (taught), ʾaḥyī (gave life/saved), ʾaglī (revealed), ʾaqrebtūn (brought near), ʾappaqnī (brought me out), ʾaḥyat (gave life), ʾaqrebtnī (brought me near)

Sentence 1

ܘܝܘܚܢܢ ܩܡ ܒܡܨܥܬ ܥܡܐ ܘܐܟܪܙ ܐܢܘܢ

w-Yukhannan qam b-meṣʿat ʿammā w-ʾkraz ʾennūn

w- (and-) Yukhannan (John) qam (rose/stood) b-meṣʿat (in-the-midst-of) ʿammā (the-people) w-ʾkraz (and-proclaimed) ʾennūn (them)

→ And Yukhannan stood in the midst of the people and proclaimed to them:

Sentence 2

ܡܪܝܐ ܫܕܪ ܠܝ ܕܐܐܠܦ ܝܬܟܘܢ ܐܘܪܚܐ ܕܚܝܐ

Māryā šadar lī d-ʾalep yātḵūn ʾūrḥā d-ḥayye

Māryā (the-Lord) šadar (sent) lī (to-me) d-ʾalep (that-I-should-teach) yātḵūn (you(pl.)) ʾūrḥā (the-way) d-ḥayye (of-life)

→ ‘The Lord has sent me to teach you the way of life.’

Sentence 3

ܐܠܗܐ ܕܒܪܐ ܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܐܚܝܝ ܠܟܘܢ ܒܦܘܪܩܢܗ

Alāhā d-brā kull medem ʾaḥyī lḵūn b-purqāneh

Alāhā (God) d-brā (who-created) kull (all) medem (thing) ʾaḥyī (caused-to-live/saved) lḵūn (you(pl.)) b-purqāneh (by-his-redemption)

→ ‘God, who created all things, has saved you through his redemption.’

Sentence 4

ܗܘ ܐܓܠܝ ܠܢ ܪܐܙܐ ܕܛܝܒܘܬܗ

Hū ʾaglī lān rāzā d-ṭaybūtteh

Hū (He) ʾaglī (revealed) lān (to-us) rāzā (the-mystery) d-ṭaybūtteh (of-his-grace)

→ ‘He has revealed to us the mystery of his grace.’

Sentence 5

ܘܗܫܐ ܐܩܪܒܬܘܢ ܠܐܠܗܐ ܒܗܝܡܢܘܬܐ

w-hāšā ʾaqrebtūn l-Alāhā b-haymānūttā

w- (and-) hāšā (now) ʾaqrebtūn (you(pl.)-have-been-brought-near) l-Alāhā (to-God) b-haymānūttā (by-faith)

→ ‘And now you have been brought near to God through faith.’

Sentence 6

ܗܢܘ ܫܪܪܐ ܕܡܠܟܘܬܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ

Hannū šrārā d-malkūttā d-Alāhā

Hannū (This-is) šrārā (the-truth) d-malkūttā (of-the-kingdom) d-Alāhā (of-God)

→ ‘This is the truth of the kingdom of God.’

Sentence 7

ܘܥܡܐ ܫܡܥ ܡܠܘܗܝ ܘܐܬܕܡܪ ܛܒ

w-ʿammā šmaʿ mellāw-hy w-ʾetdammer ṭāb

w- (and-) ʿammā (the-people) šmaʿ (heard) mellāw-hy (his-words) w-ʾetdammer (and-marveled) ṭāb (greatly/well)

→ And the people heard his words and marveled greatly.

Sentence 8

ܘܐܡܪ ܓܒܪܐ ܚܕ ܡܢ ܥܡܐ ܡܢ ܐܢܬ ܘܡܢ ܫܕܪܟ

w-ʾemar gabrā ḥad men ʿammā: man ʾant w-man šedrāḵ?

w-ʾemar (and-said) gabrā (a-man) ḥad (one) men (from) ʿammā (the-people) man (who) ʾant (are-you) w-man (and-who) šedrāḵ (sent-you)

→ And a man from the people said: ‘Who are you, and who sent you?’

Sentence 9

ܥܢܐ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܘܐܡܪ ܐܢܐ ܥܒܕܗ ܕܡܪܝܐ

ʿnā Yukhannan w-ʾemar: ʾenā ʿabdeh d-Māryā

ʿnā (answered) Yukhannan (Yukhannan) w-ʾemar (and-said) ʾenā (I) ʿabdeh (servant-of) d-Māryā (the-Lord)

→ Yukhannan answered and said: ‘I am the servant of the Lord.’

Sentence 10

ܗܘ ܐܦܩܢܝ ܡܢ ܡܕܒܪܐ ܕܐܐܠܦ ܠܥܡܗ

Hū ʾappaqnī men madbārā d-ʾalep l-ʿammeh

Hū (He) ʾappaqnī (brought-me-out) men (from) madbārā (the-wilderness) d-ʾalep (to-teach) l- (to) ʿammeh (his-people)

→ ‘He brought me out from the wilderness to teach his people.’

Sentence 11

ܘܪܘܚܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܗܝ ܕܐܚܝܬ ܠܝ ܘܐܩܪܒܬܢܝ ܠܡܠܟܘܬܗ

w-rūḥā d-Alāhā hī d-ʾaḥyat lī w-ʾaqrebtnī l-malkūtteh

w- (and-) rūḥā (the-Spirit) d-Alāhā (of-God) hī (she/it-is) d-ʾaḥyat (who-gave-life) lī (to-me) w-ʾaqrebtnī (and-brought-me-near) l-malkūtteh (to-his-kingdom)

→ ‘And it is the Spirit of God who gave me life and brought me near to his kingdom.’
In the story, what did Yukhannan say the Lord sent him to do?

answer.text: To teach the people the way of life (ʾūrḥā d-ḥayye)
To baptize the people in the river

feedback.text: The story does not mention baptism.

answer.text: To build a church in the wilderness

questiontext.text: Which Aphel verbs does Yukhannan use for God's actions in sentences 3–5?

feedback.text: These do not appear in his speech.

questiontext.text: How does Yukhannan identify himself to the man from the crowd?

answer.text: As the servant of the Lord (ʿabdeh d-Māryā)
As a prophet from the wilderness

feedback.text: He mentions the wilderness, but calls himself a servant.

answer.text: As a teacher of the law

questiontext.text: According to sentence 11, who gave Yukhannan life and brought him near the kingdom?

feedback.text: Correct: note the feminine verbs ʾaḥyat, ʾaqrebtnī, agreeing with rūḥā.

questiontext.text: Exercise 1. Identify ܐܠܦ (ʾalep).

answer.text: Aphel perfect 3 m.sg. of ʾ-l-p: 'he taught'
Peal perfect 3 m.sg. of ʾ-l-p: 'he learned'

feedback.text: The doubled l and ʾa- show the Aphel.
The participle has the m- prefix: maʾlep.

questiontext.text: Exercise 1. Identify ܡܐܠܦ (maʾlep).

feedback.text: The Peal participle has no m- prefix.

questiontext.text: Exercise 1. Identify ܟܬܒ when vocalized kāteb.

answer.text: Peal participle m.sg. of k-t-b: 'writing, writer'

questiontext.text: Exercise 1. Which of these is Peal, not Aphel?
Exercise 3. Translate: ܝܘܚܢܢ ܐܠܦ ܠܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ (Yukhannan ʾalep l-talmīdāw-hy)

feedback.text: l- marks the disciples as the object.
The perfect is past, and -āw-hy is plural.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. Which is the best Syriac for 'The Spirit brought him out of the wilderness'?

feedback.text: Correct: Aphel of the root meaning 'go out', with the object suffix.
That is the Peal: 'the Spirit went out'.
That says 'brought him near to the wilderness'.

Section 10: Grammatical Summary

THE APHEL STEM — FORMATION RULES

Feature Rule Example
Perfect prefix ʾa- (Ayin-Alaph) before root ʾa + R1 + e + R2 + suffix
Perfect 3 m.sg. ʾa + R1R2eR3 (no suffix) ʾalep, ʾaḥyī, ʾaqreb
Suffix set Same as Peal perfect -at, -t, -ti, -et, -ū, -ī, -tūn, -tin, -n
Participle prefix m- before root m + ʾ + R2 + e + R3
Participle 3 m.sg. maʾ + R2eR3 maʾlep
Participle suffixes Same as all participles -ā (f.sg.), -īn (m.pl.), -ān (f.pl.)
Core meaning Causative ‘to cause X to happen’ / ‘to make X do Y’

Meaning Pattern

PEAL (basic) + ʾa- prefix = APHEL (causative) ‘to X’ → ‘to cause to X’ / ‘to make X happen’ ḥ-y-y: live → ʾaḥyī: give life/save | q-r-b: draw near → ʾaqreb: bring near | n-p-q: go out → ʾappeq: bring out

Comparative Summary: Three Stems

Stem Meaning Perfect 3 m.sg. Participle m.sg. Translation
Peal Basic katab kāteb ‘he wrote’ / ‘writing’
Paael Intensive/Factitive qaddaš mqaddeš ‘he sanctified’ / ‘sanctifying’
Aphel Causative ʾalep maʾlep ‘he taught’ / ‘teaching’

Remember: In all three derived stems (Paael, Aphel, Ethpaael, etc.), the active participle always takes a m- prefix. This is your clearest signal that you are reading a derived-stem participle.
